los.text: Describe the the main causes, clinical signs and symptoms, likely diagnosis, investigations and treatment following trauma (focus on lower arm)
los.html:
• Mechanism: usually FOOSH (fall on outstretched hand).
    • Age matters: children → greenstick/buckle/Salter–Harris
    • young adults (high energy) → scaphoid, intra-articular
    • elderly osteoporotic women → Colles'.
InjuryFeaturesManagement
Colles' fractureDistal radius, dorsal angulation/displacement ("dinner fork")Reduce (haematoma or Bier's block) + cast; ORIF if unstable/intra-articular. Fragility fracture → DEXA/bone protection
Smith's fractureVolar displacement (fall on flexed wrist)Usually ORIF (unstable)
Barton'sIntra-articular distal radius with carpal subluxationORIF
Scaphoid fractureAnatomical snuffbox tenderness, pain on axial thumb loading; X-ray often normal initiallyScaphoid views; if suspected but X-ray normal → splint + MRI. Retrograde blood supply → avascular necrosis/non-union of proximal pole
GaleazziRadial shaft fracture + distal radioulnar joint dislocationORIF
MonteggiaUlnar shaft fracture + radial head dislocationORIF
Perilunate/lunate dislocationSevere pain, median nerve symptomsUrgent reduction
Boxer's fracture5th metacarpal neck (punch)Buddy strapping; check rotation; fight bite → antibiotics/washout
AssessmentDeformity, swelling, skin integrity (open?), neurovascular status (median nerve in distal radius fractures), X-ray two views (+ joint above and below).
ComplicationsMalunion, median nerve injury, complex regional pain syndrome, EPL tendon rupture, compartment syndrome, stiffness.

los.text: Describe the structure and function of musculoskeletal connective tissues (bone, cartilage, ligaments, tendons)
los.html:
Composition
  • Water (~60–70%)
  • Type I collagen (~80% of dry weight; tendons > ligaments)
  • Small amounts of type III/V
  • Elastin (more in ligaments)
  • Proteoglycans (decorin)
  • Fibroblasts (tenocytes in tendon).
Hierarchy
  • Tropocollagen
  • → fibril
  • → fibre
  • → fascicle (endotenon)
  • → tendon (epitenon, paratenon or synovial sheath where it changes direction, e.g. flexor tendons in hand).
MechanicsCrimped collagen straightens under low load (toe region) → linear elastic region → failure. Viscoelastic: creep, stress relaxation, rate-dependent stiffness.
TendonsTransmit muscle force to bone; store elastic energy (Achilles). Myotendinous junction and enthesis (fibrocartilaginous transition to bone) are weak points.
Ligaments
  • Bone–bone
  • Guide joint motion, resist excessive movement, proprioception (mechanoreceptors).
  • Intra-articular ligaments (ACL) heal poorly (synovial fluid, poor blood supply)
  • Extra-articular (MCL) heal well.
Healing
  • Inflammation (days) → proliferation (fibroblasts lay down type III collagen, weeks) → remodelling (type I replaces type III, months–year).
  • Repaired tissue is weaker and less organised.
  • Controlled early loading improves alignment.
PathologyTendinopathy (failed healing response, not inflammation), rupture (Achilles; fluoroquinolones and steroids increase risk), sprains (grade I–III).

los.text: Describe the neuromuscular junction and the events that lead to the generation and propagation of an action potential in skeletal muscle
los.html:
NMJMotor neuron terminal → synaptic cleft (with acetylcholinesterase in basal lamina) → motor end plate (junctional folds rich in nicotinic ACh receptors).
Sequence
  • AP arrives
  • → voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels (P/Q-type) open
  • → Ca²⁺ influx
  • → ACh vesicle exocytosis (SNARE)
  • → ACh binds nicotinic receptors (ligand-gated Na⁺/K⁺ channel)
  • → end-plate potential
  • → if threshold reached, voltage-gated Na⁺ channels in adjacent sarcolemma fire
  • → muscle AP propagates along sarcolemma and down T-tubules.
  • ACh is broken down by AChE → choline recycled.
Safety factorNormally EPP far exceeds threshold.
Disorders/drugs
  • Myasthenia gravis: antibodies vs AChR (or MuSK) → fatigable weakness (ptosis, diplopia). Rx: pyridostigmine (AChE inhibitor), immunosuppression, thymectomy.
  • Lambert–Eaton: antibodies vs presynaptic VGCC (small cell lung cancer); improves with repetition.
  • Botulinum toxin: cleaves SNARE proteins → blocks ACh release.
  • Neuromuscular blockers: non-depolarising (rocuronium: competitive antagonists; reversed by neostigmine or sugammadex) and depolarising (suxamethonium: persistent depolarisation; hyperkalaemia, malignant hyperthermia).
  • Organophosphates: irreversible AChE inhibition → cholinergic crisis.

los.text: Describe the mechanisms of skeletal and smooth muscle contraction including the process of excitation contraction coupling
los.html:
Skeletal muscle

Excitation–contraction coupling
  • AP down T-tubule
  • → DHP receptor (voltage sensor, L-type) mechanically linked to ryanodine receptor (RyR1) on sarcoplasmic reticulum
  • → Ca²⁺ release
  • → Ca²⁺ binds troponin C
  • → tropomyosin moves
  • → myosin-binding sites on actin exposed.
Cross-bridge cycle
  • Myosin head (ADP + Pi) binds actin
  • → power stroke (Pi release)
  • → ADP released
  • → ATP binds → myosin detaches (no ATP = rigor mortis)
  • → ATP hydrolysis re-cocks the head.
RelaxationSERCA pumps Ca²⁺ back into SR (needs ATP).
Sliding filamentA band constant; I band and H zone shorten; sarcomere = Z line to Z line.
Force gradationMotor unit recruitment (size principle) and summation/tetanus.
Malignant hyperthermiaRyR1 mutation + volatile anaesthetic/suxamethonium → uncontrolled Ca²⁺ release → treat with dantrolene.

Smooth muscle

  • No sarcomeres/troponin; actin anchored to dense bodies. Ca²⁺ from extracellular (L-type channels) and SR (IP₃ receptors via Gq).
  • Ca²⁺–calmodulin → myosin light-chain kinase (MLCK) → phosphorylates myosin light chain → contraction.
    • Myosin light-chain phosphatase → relaxation (activated by cGMP/NO; inhibited by Rho kinase).
  • Slow, sustained, energy-efficient (latch state); single-unit (gap junctions, gut, uterus) vs multi-unit (iris, large arteries).

los.text: Explain the perception of cue and context to the formation of health beliefs
los.html:
Placebo effect
  • Real improvement from the context of treatment rather than its pharmacological content.
  • Nocebo: negative expectations produce real harm (side effects reported on placebo; ~ "statin intolerance" often nocebo, shown in SAMSON trial).
Mechanisms
  • Expectation (cognitive): beliefs about treatment shape outcome; verbal suggestion.
  • Conditioning: previous experience of treatment (cues such as pills, injections, white coats) triggers learned responses.
  • Neurobiology: endogenous opioids (blocked by naloxone), dopamine (Parkinson's), ↓ pain-processing activity on imaging.
Cue and contextClinician warmth, confidence and empathy; branding, price, colour, size and number of pills; injections > tablets; consultation length and setting.
Health beliefs form from these cues + culture, past experience, social learning and media → influence adherence and help-seeking.
Ethics
  • Deceptive placebos conflict with honesty/autonomy
  • Open-label placebos can still work.
  • Clinicians can harness context ethically (positive framing, empathy) and reduce nocebo (careful framing of side effects).
ResearchWhy RCTs need placebo control and blinding.

los.text: Describe the principles and limitations of medical ethics (focus on Western ethics)
los.html:
Four principles(Beauchamp & Childress)
  • Autonomy: respect informed, capacitous decisions (consent, confidentiality, truth-telling).
  • Beneficence: act in the patient's best interests.
  • Non-maleficence: avoid harm (primum non nocere); balance risks/benefits.
  • Justice: fair distribution of resources, equal treatment.
Ethical theories
  • Consequentialism/utilitarianism (best outcome for greatest number)
  • Deontology (duties and rules, Kant: treat people as ends, not means)
  • Virtue ethics (what would a good doctor do: honesty, compassion)
  • Care ethics
  • Rights-based approaches.
Limitations
  • Principles conflict (autonomy vs beneficence) with no ranking
  • Abstract and hard to apply
  • Western and individualistic (may clash with family/community-centred decision-making in other cultures)
  • Utilitarianism can sacrifice individuals
  • Deontology is rigid when duties clash.
PracticeGMC Good Medical Practice, professional codes; clinical ethics committees.

los.text: Describe the principles and limitations of medical law (focus on Western law)
los.html:
Sources (England & Wales)
  • Statute (Acts of Parliament, e.g. Mental Capacity Act 2005, Human Tissue Act 2004, Abortion Act 1967)
  • Common law (case law/precedent)
  • Human rights law (Human Rights Act 1998, ECHR)
  • Regulations
  • Welsh Senedd legislation for devolved areas (health services, organ donation opt-out: Human Transplantation (Wales) Act 2013).
Civil vs criminal lawNegligence is civil (compensation); assault, gross negligence manslaughter are criminal.
Key areas
  • Consent: valid if voluntary, informed and capacitous. Montgomery (2015): disclose material risks a reasonable patient would want to know. Treating without consent = battery.
  • Negligence: duty of care + breach (Bolam test: responsible body of medical opinion; Bolitho: opinion must be logical) + causation + harm.
  • Confidentiality: common law duty; GDPR/Data Protection Act 2018; exceptions (consent, public interest, legal requirement such as notifiable diseases).
  • Capacity: MCA 2005 (presume capacity; understand, retain, weigh, communicate).
LimitationsLaw sets minimum standards (lawful ≠ ethical); slow to change; adversarial; jurisdiction-specific; costly; can promote defensive medicine.

los.text: Explain the meaning of conflict within a global context, and how this impacts on at individual and societal level
los.html:
ConflictOrganised violence between groups or states (war, civil war, terrorism, genocide), also structural violence.
Direct health impactsDeaths and injuries (blast, gunshot, landmines), sexual violence, torture.
Indirect impacts(usually larger)
  • Destruction of health systems and infrastructure (water, sanitation → cholera)
  • Attacks on healthcare workers
  • Food insecurity and malnutrition
  • Disrupted vaccination (polio, measles resurgence)
  • Loss of chronic disease care
  • Displacement into camps (overcrowding, infectious disease).
Individual levelPTSD, depression, anxiety, disability, loss of family, education and livelihood; children particularly vulnerable (child soldiers, separation).
Societal levelForced migration (refugees, internally displaced people), economic collapse, brain drain of health workers, generational trauma, breakdown of social cohesion.
Responses
  • International humanitarian law (Geneva Conventions protect medical neutrality), NGOs (MSF, ICRC), WHO
  • Refugee health in host countries (e.g. UK asylum seekers: barriers to care).
Global contextMost conflicts now intrastate; long-term disruption of SDG progress.
